summary: Unexpected throttling during concurrent GraphQL batch requests and webhook callbacks
description:
Issue summary:
Customer EchoCart reports recurrent 429 throttles during a nightly job that sends batched GraphQL requests to generate personalized product descriptions. The same job concurrently triggers webhook callbacks to a third-party image service which issues short-lived signed callbacks back to EchoCart, which in turn call our generation endpoint.

Impact:
- >50% of batch runs (approx 80k queries over 30 minutes) see mid-job 429s, causing retries and partial output.
- Client reports higher than expected token consumption for the window; customers see increased latency due to retries.

Environment:
- Dedicated tenant on prod in us-east-1; Dedicated pool id: ded-echo-07 (customer provided).
- Traffic pattern: orchestrated workers (8 parallel) submit GraphQL batch requests (size 64) while receiving webhook callbacks that immediately fire follow-up generation calls.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start 8 parallel workers that submit GraphQL batched generate requests every 5s with batch_size=64.
2) Configure webhook endpoint that replies with a signed short-lived callback to the worker that triggers an immediate follow-up generate of up to 4 small prompts.
3) Observe throttling after ~6-8 minutes into the run and sustained 429s until token buckets refill.

Observed behavior:
- Server returns 429 with X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0.
- Rate-limit headers show a short refill window (30s) and a per-route concurrency window that appears to be shared across the route and the webhook callback path.

Expected behavior:
- Batch generation and webhook-driven follow-ups should be accounted under separate route isolation or under tenant burst windows without mutual exhaustion.

Customer-provided artefacts:
- Sample request IDs: req-echo-20260310-11, req-echo-20260310-47
- Timestamps: 2026-03-09T03:12:04Z to 2026-03-09T03:45:00Z
- Representative raw headers and X-RateLimit- headers attached in ticket (snippets pasted below).
comments: 2026-03-10 - Aisha Patel: Acknowledged. Reproducing in lab to confirm quota accounting. Asked customer for pool id and example curl traces.

2026-03-11 - Customer (EchoCart support): Provided ded-echo-07, curl snippets, and sample worker orchestration script. Noted throttle starts after multiple webhook callbacks overlap with main batch window.

2026-03-12 - Marcus Liu: Reproduced locally with a reduced harness. Observed per-route token bucket showing cross-route depletion when webhook callbacks use same route key. Hypothesis: route-level isolation not applied to ephemeral callback path leading to double counting.

2026-03-13 - SRE (J. Morales): Added tracing hooks to ded-echo-07 to collect per-route accounting for the next customer run. Suggested workaround: configure callbacks to use a dedicated route or ephemeral key with isolated quota, or increase burst credits on tenant for nightly window.

2026-03-14 - Marcus Liu: Customer applied temporary mitigation by routing callbacks through a distinct API route key and saw immediate reduction in 429s. Awaiting post-run logs to confirm full resolution.
investigation_notes: Collected tenant accounting snapshots for ded-echo-07 during repro window; found two active route keys with identical route tags. Both keys counted against the same per-route concurrency window and shared burst credits.

Rate limiter config for the tenant uses a short refill window of 30s and a small burst bucket intended for interactive traffic; this pattern is incompatible with large concurrent batch windows plus many small follow-ups.

Observed that webhook callbacks come in with the same Authorization header (client reuses API key) and are therefore attributed to the same route ledger; this causes the batch request stream and callback micro-requests to compete for the same token bucket.
No evidence of proxy duplication or double-counting from our edge logs; counting appears correct but the allocation policy is suboptimal for this workload.
workaround: Customer temporary mitigation: route webhook callbacks through a separate dedicated route key or use a secondary API key for callbacks so traffic is accounted separately. Alternative short-term fix: increase tenant burst credits for nightly window or increase refill window to 2m.
next_steps: Recommend config change: create route-level isolation for webhook callback endpoint (route tag: echo-webhook-cb) and assign a separate quota/burst profile.
Product: evaluate default refill windows for dedicated tenants running mixed batch+realtime patterns; consider adaptive refill for bursty batch windows.
SRE: monitor ded-echo-07 in next scheduled run and collect per-route bucket histograms; correlate with latency and retry counts.
Follow-up: if customer prefers product-side change, open INT ticket to propose a new quota profile for mixed batch workloads.
resolution: Partial workaround applied by customer (separate route key for callbacks) and confirmed immediate improvement in subsequent short runs. Ownership: SRE to validate in scheduled nightly full run before closing. No code change required yet.
customer_feedback: EchoCart reports that after applying the separate callback key the 429s dropped from ~60% of jobs to <5% during short tests; they will run full nightly cadence and report back.
estimated_customer_impact: High - nightly generation job failures and retry costs; observed increased token spend and delayed downstream consumer processing.
notes_for_engineering: Consider adding a docs note for dedicated customers describing common pitfall: shared API key across primary batch route and synchronous webhook callbacks can exhaust short-window burst quotas. Recommend adding an example config in the console templates for separating callback traffic.
